definition: to stick firmly to a surface, or to follow a rule or belief closely

examples.text: The gecko's feet adhere to glass through millions of microscopic hairs.
The colony adhered to the old calendar for decades after the capital had changed it.
If you adhere to the recipe exactly, the bread rises every time.

confused.note: To adhere is the verb; an adhesive is a substance that makes things stick.

questions.passage: The orchestra's founder insisted that players ______ strictly to the composer's markings. Any musician who slowed down where the score did not call for it could expect a sharp look from the podium.
questions.explanation: Following the markings strictly means sticking closely to them.

distractors.why: Deviate means to stray from, which is exactly what the founder forbade.
Allude means to refer to indirectly, which does not fit following a score.
Succumb means to give in to pressure or temptation, the wrong idea for obeying instructions.

definition: determined and firm in purpose

examples.text: The resolute defenders held the bridge for three days against a far larger force.
She is resolute in her refusal to sell the family orchard.
I was resolute about finishing the marathon, even if I had to walk the last mile.

confused.note: Resolute is the adjective; a resolution is a firm decision or the solving of a problem.

questions.passage: Friends urged the climber to abandon her attempt after two failed tries and a broken wrist. She remained ______, training through the winter and returning to the mountain the following spring.
questions.explanation: Training on and returning after setbacks shows firm determination.

distractors.why: Fickle means changing one's mind easily, but she never wavered.
Apprehensive means worried, which does not describe her persistence.
Complacent means self-satisfied and no longer trying; she trained all winter.

definition: not harmful or offensive

examples.text: Most bacteria on the skin are innocuous, and many are helpful.
An innocuous remark about the weather starts the quarrel that ends the friendship.
The spider in the shower looked scary but was completely innocuous.

confused.note: Innocuous means harmless; innocent means not guilty or not experienced.

questions.passage: The mushroom looks almost identical to a deadly species that grows in the same forests. It is, however, entirely ______, and foragers who learn to tell the two apart can eat it safely.
questions.explanation: A mushroom that can be eaten safely is harmless.

distractors.why: Noxious means harmful or poisonous, which describes the look-alike.
Ephemeral means short-lived, which is not the point of the contrast.
Conspicuous means easy to notice, which says nothing about safety.

definition: to emphasize or show the importance of something

examples.text: The outbreak underscores the need for faster testing.
The disaster underscored how poorly the city's levees had been maintained.
The flat tire underscored why Dad always tells us to check the spare.

confused.note: Underscore means to emphasize; undermine means to weaken.

questions.passage: The report's authors could have described water shortages only in general terms. Instead, they open with the story of a town that trucked in drinking water for a year, a choice that ______ how urgent the problem has become.
questions.explanation: A vivid example emphasizes the urgency.

distractors.why: Undermines means weakens; the example strengthens the sense of urgency.
Refutes means disproves, but the story supports the authors' point.
Rescinds means officially cancels, which makes no sense here.

definition: done without good reason; unnecessary and unwelcome

examples.text: Reviewers objected to the film's gratuitous explosions, which added nothing to the plot.
The gratuitous destruction of the library shocked even the general's allies.
His gratuitous comment about my shoes was not helpful.

confused.note: Gratuitous means uncalled for; gratitude is thankfulness.

questions.passage: The biography is thorough, but it is marred by ______ insults. In a chapter on the scientist's early research, for instance, the author pauses to mock a rival's haircut, a detail that serves no purpose.
questions.explanation: An insult that serves no purpose is unnecessary and unwarranted.

distractors.why: Judicious means showing good sense, which pointless insults do not.
Subtle means delicate and hard to notice; mocking a haircut is neither.
Inadvertent means accidental, but the author pauses on purpose to mock.

definition: not clear; vague or without definite form

examples.text: The boundary between the two species is nebulous, since they sometimes interbreed.
He has only a nebulous memory of the house where he was born.
The plan for spring break is still nebulous; all we know is "somewhere warm."

confused.note: A nebula is a cloud of gas in space; nebulous means cloudy in the sense of vague.

questions.passage: Voters complained that the candidate's promises were ______. He spoke often of "a brighter tomorrow" and "real change" but never said which laws he would pass or how he would pay for them.
questions.explanation: Slogans with no specifics are vague.

distractors.why: Explicit means clearly stated, which his promises were not.
Exorbitant means unreasonably costly; the complaint is about vagueness.
Nefarious means wicked, a far harsher charge than being unclear.

definition: using few words, sometimes in a way that seems unfriendly

examples.text: Hemingway's terse sentences leave much for the reader to supply.
The admiral's terse message read simply, "Enemy sighted."
Her terse "fine" made it clear that things were not fine.

confused.note: Terse means brief and clipped; tense means stretched tight or nervous.

questions.passage: The director is known for long, enthusiastic emails. So when her reply to the proposal consisted of the ______ line "Not now," the team suspected that something was wrong.
questions.explanation: A two-word reply is brief and clipped.

distractors.why: Verbose means wordy, which describes her usual emails.
Effusive means gushing with feeling, the opposite of "Not now."
Nebulous means vague; the reply was short but clear.

definition: to describe or mark something clearly and exactly

examples.text: The treaty delineated the border along the crest of the mountains.
The paper delineates the three stages of the insect's life cycle.
The syllabus delineates exactly what counts toward the final grade.

confused.note: Delineate means to mark out clearly; delegate means to assign a task to someone.

questions.passage: Disputes between the two departments arose because nobody knew who was responsible for what. The new handbook solves this by carefully ______ each department's duties in a two-page chart.
questions.explanation: A chart that sets out each department's duties marks them clearly.

distractors.why: Obscuring means making unclear, which would worsen the disputes.
Rescinding means cancelling, but the handbook defines duties and does not remove them.
Lamenting means expressing sorrow, which a chart cannot do.

definition: bitter, long-lasting anger or resentment

examples.text: The rancor between the two families outlived everyone who remembered its cause.
He speaks of his former partner without rancor, which surprises his listeners.
Even years later, there was rancor in her voice when she mentioned the group project.

confused.note: Rancor is bitter resentment; rancid describes spoiled food.

questions.passage: The two scientists had competed for the same prize for a decade. Yet when one finally won, the other congratulated her without a trace of ______, saying the committee had made the right choice.
questions.explanation: Warm congratulations show no bitterness or resentment.

distractors.why: Deference means respectful yielding; the sentence stresses the absence of bitterness.
Candor means honesty; saying he spoke "without a trace of honesty" would undercut his praise.
Acumen means sharp judgment, which is not what a gracious loser would lack.

definition: using very few words

examples.text: The Spartans were famous for laconic replies to long-winded threats.
The laconic cowboy answers every question with "Yep" or "Nope."
My laconic grandfather can sum up a two-hour movie in four words.

confused.note: Laconic means using few words; lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy.

questions.passage: Unlike her predecessor, who filled every press conference with long stories, the new coach is ______. Asked how the team had prepared for the final, she said only, "We practiced."
questions.explanation: A two-word answer shows she uses very few words.

distractors.why: Loquacious means very talkative, which describes her predecessor.
Belligerent means hostile; her answer was short, not aggressive.
Effusive means pouring out words and feeling, the opposite of her style.

partsNote: from Laconia, the region of Sparta

definition: empty, bare, and without people; or very sad and alone

examples.text: The rover crossed a desolate plain of red dust and scattered rock.
After her brother leaves, the house feels desolate.
The beach is desolate in January, with only gulls for company.

confused.note: Desolate means empty or miserable; dissolute means lacking moral restraint.

questions.passage: Travelers who expected a thriving port were dismayed by what they found. The harbor was ______: the warehouses stood empty, weeds grew through the docks, and not a single ship lay at anchor.
questions.explanation: Empty warehouses, weeds, and no ships describe a bare, deserted place.

distractors.why: Opulent means rich and luxurious, the opposite of an abandoned harbor.
Tranquil means pleasantly calm, but the travelers were dismayed.
Gregarious means sociable, a word for people, not harbors.

definition: to hate something very strongly

examples.text: The reformer abhorred slavery and spent her fortune fighting it.
The hero abhors lying, which makes his final deception all the more painful.
I abhor the sound of a fork scraping a plate.

confused.note: Abhor and adore are opposites that look alike: abhor means to hate, adore means to love.

questions.passage: The editor ______ clichés. She would strike "at the end of the day" from any manuscript on sight and was said to have returned one article with every instance of "game changer" circled in red.
questions.explanation: Striking and circling clichés on sight shows strong hatred of them.

distractors.why: Condoned means allowed or overlooked, which she never did.
Extolled means praised highly, the opposite of her attitude.
Emulated means imitated, but she removed clichés from writing.

definition: originating in or belonging naturally to a particular place

examples.text: The kiwi is indigenous to New Zealand and is found nowhere else in the wild.
Indigenous peoples of the region farmed these terraces long before the empire arrived.
The garden center sells indigenous plants that need no extra watering.

confused.note: Indigenous means native; indigent means very poor.

questions.passage: Gardeners are often advised to choose ______ plants. Because such species evolved in the local climate, they usually need less water and resist local pests better than varieties brought in from other regions.
questions.explanation: Species that evolved in the local climate are native to the place.

distractors.why: Exotic means from a distant place, the kind of plant the advice warns against.
Indigent means poor; it only resembles the right word.
Ornate means richly decorated, which does not explain needing less water.

definition: certain to happen and impossible to avoid

examples.text: Given the fault's history, another large earthquake is inevitable.
Once the grain ships stopped arriving, famine in the city was inevitable.
With six cousins and one piñata, tears were inevitable.

confused.note: Inevitable means unavoidable; inedible means not fit to eat.

questions.passage: Looking back, historians often describe the empire's collapse as ______. At the time, however, few observers saw it coming, and many believed that reforms could still save the state.
questions.explanation: "However" contrasts hindsight, in which collapse seems certain, with how it looked then.

distractors.why: Fortuitous means happening by lucky chance, which does not fit a collapse.
Gratuitous means uncalled for, which is not the contrast with "few saw it coming."
Innocuous means harmless, which a collapse is not.

definition: to admit that something is true, often unwillingly; to give up or yield

examples.text: After the final count, the governor conceded the election by telegram.
Even the theory's critics concede that it explains the fossil record well.
I had to concede that my sister's shortcut really was faster.

confused.note: Concede means to admit or yield; conceive means to form an idea.

questions.passage: The author argues that cities should ban cars from their centers. She does ______, however, that such bans can hurt small shops in the short term, and she devotes a chapter to ways of softening that blow.
questions.explanation: She admits a point that works against her own argument.

distractors.why: Deny means to say something is untrue, but she goes on to address the problem.
Gloat means to take smug pleasure, the wrong tone for admitting a drawback.
Fabricate means to invent falsely, which she does not do.

partsNote: to go along with, to yield

definition: the highest point of success or development

examples.text: Under that emperor, the dynasty reached the pinnacle of its power.
Critics regard her third novel as the pinnacle of her career.
Winning the state title was the pinnacle of our season.

confused.note: A pinnacle is a peak; pinochle is a card game.

questions.passage: Many athletes consider an Olympic gold medal the ______ of their sport. For the marathoner Kiptum, however, the greater achievement was a world record set on an ordinary city course.
questions.explanation: A gold medal is treated as the highest achievement.

distractors.why: Nadir means the lowest point, the opposite of a gold medal.
Antithesis means the direct opposite, which a medal is not.
A precursor is something that comes before and leads to another thing, not a crowning achievement.

definition: drawing on a wide variety of sources or styles

examples.text: Her eclectic reading ranges from comic books to medieval sermons.
The palace is an eclectic mix of Persian arches and Roman columns.
My playlist is eclectic: opera, hip-hop, and whale sounds.

confused.note: Eclectic means varied in sources; it has no connection to electricity.

questions.passage: The restaurant's menu is ______, to say the least. Diners can order Korean dumplings, Sicilian pasta, and Peruvian ceviche at the same table, and the dessert list borrows from at least five more countries.
questions.explanation: Dishes from many cuisines show a wide variety of sources.

distractors.why: Homogeneous means all of one kind, the opposite of this menu.
Austere means severely plain, which such a varied menu is not.
Banal means boringly unoriginal, which does not fit so unusual a mix.

definition: a strong feeling of dislike that makes you avoid something

examples.text: Rats quickly develop an aversion to any food that once made them ill.
The narrator's aversion to crowds keeps him away from his own wedding feast.
I have an aversion to phone calls and will text for an hour to avoid one.

confused.note: An aversion is a strong dislike; adversity is hardship.

questions.passage: The painter's ______ to publicity was legendary. She declined every interview, refused to attend her own exhibitions, and once left a party by the kitchen door when a photographer arrived.
questions.explanation: Avoiding interviews, exhibitions, and photographers shows a strong dislike.

distractors.why: A penchant is a strong liking, the opposite of her avoidance.
Adversity means hardship; it looks similar but does not mean dislike.
Alacrity means eager readiness, which she did not show toward publicity.

definition: trying to seem more important, clever, or cultured than you really are

examples.text: The critic mocked the novel's pretentious title, a line of untranslated Latin.
The mayor's pretentious new residence, with its forty rooms, angered taxpayers.
Calling a grilled cheese "an artisanal melted sandwich" is a bit pretentious.

confused.note: Pretentious means showing off; portentous means ominous or self-importantly solemn.

questions.passage: Reviewers found the café more ______ than pleasant. Its menu described water as "hand-poured," its staff corrected customers' pronunciation of "croissant," and a sign at the door asked guests to "respect the silence of the bean."
questions.explanation: Fancy labels for water and correcting customers show an effort to seem refined.

distractors.why: Unassuming means modest, which this café is not.
Innocuous means harmless; reviewers were irritated by the showiness.
Desolate means empty and bleak, which the passage does not describe.

definition: suggesting that future success is likely

examples.text: A clear sky on coronation day was taken as an auspicious sign.
The first trial's results were auspicious enough to justify a larger study.
Finding a parking spot right by the door was an auspicious start to the trip.

confused.note: Auspicious means promising; suspicious means distrustful or arousing distrust.

questions.passage: The young company's first week could hardly have been more ______. Its product sold out in two days, a major newspaper praised it, and three investors called to offer funding.
questions.explanation: Selling out, praise, and investor interest promise future success.

distractors.why: Ominous means threatening, the opposite of such a good start.
Mundane means ordinary, but this week was exceptional.
Suspicious means arousing distrust; it resembles the right word but has a different meaning.

partsNote: from Latin for "bird watcher," one who read omens

definition: to make a process happen more quickly

examples.text: The new railway expedited the delivery of mail to the western territories.
Automated sorting expedites the analysis of thousands of blood samples.
Paying extra will expedite your passport, but it still takes two weeks.

confused.note: Expedite is a verb meaning to speed up; expedient is an adjective meaning convenient, sometimes at the cost of what is right.

questions.passage: Applications for building permits once took six months to review. To ______ the process, the city now lets architects submit plans online, where three departments can examine them at the same time.
questions.explanation: Simultaneous online review is meant to speed the process up.

distractors.why: Impede means to slow or block, the opposite of the city's goal.
Scrutinize means to examine closely; the goal stated is speed.
Delineate means to describe or mark out, which is not the purpose of the change.

partsNote: from Latin pes, "foot": to free the feet

definition: the exact opposite of something

examples.text: Calm and patient, the heroine is the antithesis of her fiery sister.
The plain meeting house was the antithesis of the cathedrals the settlers had left behind.
A quiet cabin is the antithesis of my usual noisy apartment.

confused.note: Antithesis is the opposite of an idea; synthesis is a combination of ideas into a whole.

questions.passage: The two brothers ran the family business in sharply different ways. Marcus was cautious, quiet, and methodical; Leo, who took wild risks and loved an audience, was his ______.
questions.explanation: Leo's traits are the direct opposite of Marcus's.

distractors.why: A precedent is an earlier example, not an opposite.
A pinnacle is a high point, which does not describe a contrast between brothers.
An accolade is an honor, which does not fit.

definition: willing to take bold risks; daring

examples.text: The audacious night raid captured the fort without a single shot.
The thief's audacious plan is to rob the museum during its own gala.
It was audacious to ask the principal for a second snow day, but it worked.

confused.note: Audacious means daring; auspicious means promising.

questions.passage: Most first-time directors begin with a small, safe project. Okoro's debut was far more ______: a three-hour epic filmed on four continents with a cast of two thousand.
questions.explanation: A huge, risky first film is bold and daring.

distractors.why: Timid means lacking boldness, which describes a small, safe project.
Perfunctory means done with minimal effort, which a three-hour epic is not.
Conventional means usual, but most beginners do the opposite of what she did.

definition: the ability to judge quickly and well, especially in practical matters

examples.text: The merchant's business acumen turned one ship into a fleet of forty.
The detective's acumen lets her read a whole life in a muddy boot.
My aunt's financial acumen is why everyone asks her before buying a car.

confused.note: Acumen is sharp judgment; acme is the highest point.

questions.passage: The gallery's founder had no formal training in art history. What she did have was commercial ______: she could tell at a glance which unknown painters would be in demand a decade later.
questions.explanation: Spotting future demand at a glance shows sharp practical judgment.

distractors.why: Rancor means bitterness, which has nothing to do with judging art.
Aversion means strong dislike, which would not explain her success.
Brevity means shortness, which does not fit.

definition: never changing and impossible to change

examples.text: For centuries the stars were thought to be immutable.
The priests taught that the ancient laws were immutable.
It is an immutable rule in our house that the cook does not wash the dishes.

confused.note: Immutable means cannot be changed; immovable means cannot be moved.

questions.passage: Early geologists assumed that the continents were ______, fixed in place since the planet formed. The theory of plate tectonics overturned that assumption by showing that landmasses drift a few centimeters each year.
questions.explanation: Continents thought to be fixed since the planet formed were believed unchangeable.

distractors.why: Malleable means easily shaped or changed, the opposite of the old assumption.
Ephemeral means short-lived, the opposite of fixed forever.
Eclectic means drawn from varied sources, which does not apply.

definition: used so often that it no longer has interest or force

examples.text: The poem avoids trite images of hearts and roses.
The candidate's speech recycled trite slogans from three earlier campaigns.
"Follow your dreams" sounded trite, but I had no better advice to give.

confused.note: Trite means overused; terse means brief.

questions.passage: The graduation speaker promised to avoid the usual advice. He then spent twenty minutes telling students that life is a journey and that failure is a teacher, remarks so ______ that several listeners recited them along with him.
questions.explanation: Remarks listeners can recite along are worn out from overuse.

distractors.why: Cryptic means puzzling, but everyone already knew these lines.
Audacious means daring, which familiar advice is not.
Nebulous means vague; the problem here is overuse, not vagueness.

definition: clear, sharp, and direct in thought or expression

examples.text: Her incisive question exposed the flaw in the experiment's design.
The critic's incisive essay explains in three pages what others needed a book to say.
My debate partner's incisive reply ended the argument in one sentence.

confused.note: Incisive means sharply insightful; decisive means able to decide quickly or settling an outcome.

questions.passage: The review is admired for its ______ analysis. In a few paragraphs the critic identifies exactly why the film's second half fails, a problem that other writers had sensed but could not explain.
questions.explanation: Pinpointing what others could not explain shows sharp, clear analysis.

distractors.why: Trite means overused and unoriginal, but this analysis found something new.
Verbose means wordy, yet the critic needed only a few paragraphs.
Tentative means hesitant, but the critic identifies the problem exactly.

definition: clever skill in deceiving people

examples.text: Odysseus defeats the giant by guile, not by strength.
The envoy used guile to learn the size of the enemy fleet over dinner.
With some guile, my little sister convinced Dad that bedtime had been moved to ten.

confused.note: Guile is cunning; a guise is an outward appearance or disguise.

questions.passage: The fox in the fable cannot outrun the hounds, so it relies on ______. It doubles back along its own trail, wades down a stream to hide its scent, and leaves the dogs circling an empty thicket.
questions.explanation: Doubling back and hiding its scent are clever tricks.

distractors.why: Candor means honesty, the opposite of trickery.
Rancor means bitterness, which does not describe an escape.
Deference means respectful submission, which a fleeing fox does not show.

definition: to support or strengthen an argument, idea, or structure

examples.text: Masons buttressed the cathedral wall after cracks appeared in the stone.
The authors buttress their claim with data from twelve countries.
I buttressed my request for a raise with a list of everything I had fixed that year.

confused.note: Both mean to support; buttress suggests a solid structure of evidence, like the stone supports on a cathedral wall.

questions.passage: The historian's claim that the city traded with distant ports might have seemed speculative. She ______ it, however, with customs records, shipwreck inventories, and coins minted three thousand miles away.
questions.explanation: Records, inventories, and coins strengthen the claim.

distractors.why: Undermines means weakens, but the evidence supports her.
Concedes means admits reluctantly; she is defending her claim, not giving it up.
Satirizes means mocks through humor, which a historian would not do to her own claim.

definition: to make an unpleasant feeling less painful or severe

examples.text: The king's apology did little to assuage the anger of the exiled nobles.
Nothing could assuage her guilt over the letter she had never answered.
A glass of cold water assuaged my thirst after the long hike.

confused.note: Assuage means to soothe a feeling; persuade means to convince.

questions.passage: Investors were alarmed when the company's founder resigned without warning. To ______ their fears, the board announced within hours that an experienced successor had already been chosen.
questions.explanation: A quick announcement of a successor was meant to calm investors' fears.

distractors.why: Aggravate means to make worse, which the board did not intend.
Underscore means to emphasize; the board wanted to reduce the fears, not highlight them.
Delineate means to describe precisely, which is not the board's purpose.

definition: to praise highly, especially in public

examples.text: Newspapers lauded the engineer who had finished the bridge a year early.
Colleagues lauded the study for the size and care of its sample.
The principal lauded the robotics team at the morning assembly.

confused.note: To laud is to praise in words; to applaud is to clap or, more loosely, to approve.

questions.passage: The mayor's plan to turn an abandoned rail line into a park was not universally welcomed. Environmental groups ______ it as visionary, but nearby business owners worried about losing parking.
questions.explanation: Calling the plan visionary is high praise, in contrast to the owners' worry.

distractors.why: Denounced means condemned, but the groups called it visionary.
Rescinded means officially cancelled, which outside groups cannot do to a plan.
Belittled means made to seem unimportant, the opposite of calling it visionary.

definition: to criticize someone or something unfairly, making it seem less valuable

examples.text: Court poets denigrated the fallen minister they had flattered a month before.
The older writers denigrate her novels as "mere entertainment."
You can prefer your own school without denigrating ours.

confused.note: Denigrate means to belittle unfairly; deny means to say something is not true.

questions.passage: Supporters of the older technique were not content to defend it. They went further and ______ the new method, describing it in journals as "a toy for amateurs" despite evidence that it produced more accurate results.
questions.explanation: Calling an accurate method "a toy for amateurs" is unfair belittling.

distractors.why: Lauded means praised, the opposite of their insults.
Adopted means took up and used, which the old technique's supporters refused to do.
Assuaged means soothed a feeling, which does not apply to a method.

definition: slow and relaxed, with little energy

examples.text: The afternoon passes in languid talk on the shaded porch.
In the heat of midday the lizards grow languid and barely move.
After the huge holiday meal, everyone was too languid to clear the table.

confused.note: Languid is an adjective meaning slow and relaxed; languish is a verb meaning to grow weak or be neglected.

questions.passage: The river is nothing like the rushing torrent that visitors expect. In late summer it becomes ______, drifting so slowly past the willows that a leaf dropped from the bridge seems hardly to move.
questions.explanation: A river drifting so slowly that a leaf hardly moves is slow and unhurried.

distractors.why: Turbulent means rough and fast, which describes the torrent visitors expect.
Incisive means sharp in thought, a word for minds, not rivers.
Audacious means daring, which a slow river is not.

definition: using more words than are needed

examples.text: The editor trimmed the verbose opening from forty pages to four.
The verbose treaty ran to two hundred clauses, many of them repeating one another.
My verbose email could have been one sentence: "Running late."

confused.note: Verbose means wordy; verbal means relating to words or spoken.

questions.passage: The instructions for assembling the bookshelf are needlessly ______. A step that could be stated as "attach side panel with four screws" takes up most of a page, complete with a history of the screw's design.
questions.explanation: A page for a one-line step uses far more words than needed.

distractors.why: Terse means brief, the opposite of a page-long step.
Laconic means using very few words, which these instructions do not.
Cryptic means puzzlingly brief or obscure; these instructions are too long, not too mysterious.

definition: quick and rude in manner or speech

examples.text: The innkeeper's brusque "No rooms" sends the travelers back into the rain.
The general's brusque manner offended the diplomats he was sent to charm.
The clerk was brusque, sliding my change across the counter without a word.

confused.note: Brusque means rudely abrupt; brisk means quick and energetic in a good way.

questions.passage: Patients praised the surgeon's skill but not her bedside manner. She was ______ to the point of rudeness, answering questions with a single word and leaving the room before families had finished speaking.
questions.explanation: One-word answers and walking out mid-conversation are abrupt and rude.

distractors.why: Affable means friendly and easy to talk to, which she was not.
Verbose means wordy, but she answered in single words.
Diffident means shy; her manner was curt, not timid.

definition: tending to be quiet and to say very little

examples.text: The taciturn ferryman rows them across without answering a single question.
The taciturn president was nicknamed "Silent Cal" by reporters who could not get him to talk.
My taciturn uncle communicates mostly through nods and the occasional shrug.

confused.note: Taciturn describes a person who says little; tacit describes something understood without being said.

questions.passage: The lighthouse keeper was a ______ man. Visitors who rowed out to the rock reported that in a whole afternoon he might say no more than "Mind the step" and "Tide's turning."
questions.explanation: Speaking only a few words in an afternoon shows a habit of saying little.

distractors.why: Garrulous means excessively talkative, the opposite of the keeper.
Brusque means rudely abrupt; the keeper is merely quiet, and his few words are helpful warnings.
Pretentious means showing off, which a man of few words does not do.

definition: to warn or scold someone firmly but gently

examples.text: The bishop admonished the king to remember his oath to the people.
The nurse admonishes the children not to wake the baby.
The librarian admonished us for whispering too loudly.

confused.note: To admonish is to warn or scold gently; to berate is to scold angrily and at length.

questions.passage: The lifeguard did not shout or blow her whistle. She simply walked over and quietly ______ the swimmers, reminding them that the rocks beyond the rope were slippery and that the tide was coming in.
questions.explanation: A quiet, firm reminder of danger is a gentle warning.

distractors.why: Harangued means lectured loudly and at length, far too strong for a quiet reminder.
Lauded means praised, which is not what a warning does.
Placated means calmed someone's anger, but the swimmers were not angry.

definition: so strong or obvious that it can almost be touched or felt

examples.text: The tension in the courtroom is palpable as the jury files back in.
The patient had a palpable lump just below the collarbone.
The excitement in the gym was palpable before the final match.

confused.note: Palpable means easily felt or noticed; palatable means pleasant to taste or acceptable.

questions.passage: No one in the control room spoke as the lander began its descent. The anxiety was ______: engineers gripped their desks, and one reporter later wrote that she could "feel the air tighten."
questions.explanation: Anxiety that a reporter could feel in the air is strong enough to be sensed physically.

distractors.why: Negligible means too slight to matter, the opposite of such intense anxiety.
Spurious means fake, but the anxiety was real.
Palatable means pleasant or acceptable; it only resembles the right word.

definition: changing often and suddenly, especially in loyalty or affection

examples.text: The fickle crowd cheers the hero in one scene and jeers him in the next.
Fickle allies abandoned the duke the moment his gold ran out.
Spring weather here is fickle: sunshine at noon, hail by two.

confused.note: Fickle means changeable; feckless means irresponsible and ineffective.

questions.passage: Fashion is notoriously ______. A style of shoe that every shopper demands in March may sit unsold on clearance racks by August, replaced by something its fans would have laughed at a year earlier.
questions.explanation: Tastes that reverse within months change often and suddenly.

distractors.why: Immutable means unchanging, the opposite of fashion as described.
Resolute means firmly determined, which shifting tastes are not.
Benign means harmless, which does not address changeability.

definition: hostile and eager to fight or argue

examples.text: The belligerent nations refused every offer of mediation.
The belligerent sailor picks a quarrel with every stranger at the inn.
The driver became belligerent when the officer asked him to move his car.

confused.note: Belligerent means hostile; benevolent means kind.

questions.passage: The meeting was meant to settle the dispute calmly. Instead, one delegate arrived in a ______ mood, pounding the table, interrupting every speaker, and threatening to walk out before the agenda had even been read.
questions.explanation: Pounding the table and making threats show hostility and eagerness to fight.

distractors.why: Conciliatory means trying to make peace, the opposite of his behavior.
Languid means slow and relaxed, which table-pounding is not.
Taciturn means saying little, but he interrupted every speaker.

definition: wicked or criminal

examples.text: The count's nefarious scheme involves a forged will and a locked tower.
The pirate's nefarious career ended at the gallows in 1718.
I assumed my brother had some nefarious reason for being nice to me, and I was right.

confused.note: Nefarious means wicked; nebulous means vague.

questions.passage: At first investigators thought the missing funds were the result of sloppy bookkeeping. They later uncovered something far more ______: a deliberate plan, years in the making, to steal from the charity's donors.
questions.explanation: A deliberate, long-planned theft from a charity is wicked and criminal.

distractors.why: Innocuous means harmless, which is the opposite of a plan to steal.
Inadvertent means accidental, but the plan was deliberate.
Trite means overused, which does not describe a crime.

definition: something that departs from what is normal or expected, usually in an unwelcome way

examples.text: The cold July was an aberration in a decade of record heat.
Historians see the brief return to monarchy as an aberration in the republic's story.
My one failed quiz was an aberration, not a trend.

confused.note: An aberration is a departure from the normal; an abrasion is a scrape.

questions.passage: The team had won forty straight home games before last night's loss. Fans insisted that the defeat was an ______ and predicted that the winning would resume next week.
questions.explanation: One loss after forty wins is a departure from the normal pattern.

distractors.why: An accolade is an honor, which a loss is not.
Antithesis means the direct opposite of something, not a one-time exception.
A precedent is an example that sets a pattern, but fans say this loss will not be repeated.

partsNote: from Latin errare, "to wander": wandering away

definition: very rich and luxurious

examples.text: The sultan received ambassadors in an opulent hall lined with silk and gold.
The novel contrasts the opulent mansion on the hill with the cottages below.
The hotel lobby was so opulent that I felt underdressed in sneakers.

confused.note: Opulent means luxurious; opaque means not see-through or hard to understand.

questions.passage: The railway magnate spared no expense on his private car. Its ______ interior featured velvet armchairs, crystal lamps, a marble bathtub, and a dining table set with solid silver.
questions.explanation: Velvet, crystal, marble, and silver describe rich luxury.

distractors.why: Austere means severely plain, the opposite of this interior.
Desolate means empty and bleak, which a richly furnished car is not.
Innocuous means harmless, which says nothing about luxury.

definition: a person who attacks widely accepted beliefs, customs, or institutions

examples.text: The young iconoclast argued that the academy's rules were strangling art.
Once dismissed as an iconoclast, she lived to see her theory in every textbook.
My aunt, the family iconoclast, serves lasagna on Thanksgiving.

confused.note: An icon is a revered image or symbol; an iconoclast is someone who attacks what others revere.

questions.passage: Architects of the period agreed that a serious building needed columns and a symmetrical front. Wright, an ______ from the start of his career, rejected both, designing low, sprawling houses that seemed to grow out of the prairie.
questions.explanation: Rejecting what all his peers accepted makes him an attacker of established beliefs.

distractors.why: A conformist follows accepted practice, the opposite of Wright.
A benefactor is someone who gives help or money, which is not the point.
A novice is a beginner; the sentence is about his defiance of convention.

definition: to charm someone, sometimes in order to trick them

examples.text: The stranger beguiles the villagers with tales of a city paved in silver.
The envoy beguiled the court with gifts while his army crossed the border.
The puppy's sad eyes beguiled me into handing over half my sandwich.

confused.note: Guile is the noun for cunning; to beguile is to charm someone, sometimes by using guile.

questions.passage: The salesman never raised his voice or pressed for a decision. He ______ customers with jokes and compliments until, almost without noticing, they had agreed to buy the most expensive model on the floor.
questions.explanation: Charming people into buying without their noticing is winning them over, with a hint of trickery.

distractors.why: Admonished means warned or scolded, which would not sell anything.
Harangued means lectured loudly, but he never raised his voice.
Denigrated means belittled, but he flattered his customers.

definition: strongly supporting one side, party, or cause, often without considering others fairly

examples.text: Partisan newspapers of the 1790s printed insults that would shock modern readers.
The agency's reports are trusted because they are not partisan.
I am too partisan to referee a game when my sister's team is playing.

confused.note: Partisan means one-sided in support; a partition is a divider.

questions.passage: The committee was supposed to weigh the evidence fairly. Critics charged that its report was openly ______, noting that it accepted every claim made by one political party and dismissed every claim made by the other.
questions.explanation: Accepting one party's claims and rejecting the other's is one-sided.

distractors.why: Impartial means fair to all sides, which is what the committee failed to be.
Tentative means hesitant or provisional; the report's fault was favoritism.
Laconic means brief, which is unrelated to fairness.

partsNote: from "part": taking a part or side

definition: an earlier action or decision that serves as an example or rule for later ones

examples.text: Washington set a precedent by stepping down after two terms.
There was no precedent for approving a drug after so short a trial.
If we let the dog on the couch once, it sets a precedent.

confused.note: A precedent is an earlier example; a president is a leader.

questions.passage: The judge acknowledged that no earlier court had faced quite the same question. Lacking any ______ to guide her, she wrote that she would have to reason from the basic purpose of the law itself.
questions.explanation: An earlier ruling on the same question would serve as a guide.

distractors.why: An aberration is a departure from the norm, not a guide.
Guile means cunning deceit, which a judge would not seek as guidance.
Rancor means bitterness, which does not fit.

definition: likely to be affected or harmed by something

examples.text: Young trees are especially susceptible to frost damage.
Crowded ports were susceptible to outbreaks carried by arriving ships.
I am susceptible to any ad that features a puppy.

confused.note: Susceptible means easily affected; suspicious means distrustful.

questions.passage: Because the island's birds evolved without any ground predators, they never learned to hide their nests. This has left them highly ______ to the rats that arrived on ships in the nineteenth century.
questions.explanation: Birds with unhidden nests are easily harmed by rats.

distractors.why: Impervious means not affected, the opposite of birds with exposed nests.
Belligerent means hostile; the birds are victims, not aggressors.
Oblivious means unaware; "oblivious to the rats" would describe attention, but the sentence is about being harmed.

partsNote: able to be taken from below

definition: gentle and kind, or not harmful

examples.text: The scan showed that the growth was benign and needed no treatment.
The old gardener watches the children with a benign smile.
The dog's bark is alarming, but he is completely benign.

confused.note: Benign means harmless or kindly; malign means harmful, or as a verb, to speak ill of.

questions.passage: Residents panicked when a strange orange foam appeared along the shore. Tests soon showed that it was ______, the product of a harmless algae that blooms briefly each spring.
questions.explanation: Foam from a harmless algae poses no danger.

distractors.why: Noxious means harmful or poisonous, which the tests ruled out.
Nefarious means wicked, a word for schemes and people, not algae.
Palpable means able to be felt, which does not answer whether the foam is dangerous.

definition: disagreement and conflict between people

examples.text: Discord among the allied generals delayed the attack by a month.
The inheritance sows discord among the four sisters.
The choice of movie caused surprising discord on family night.

confused.note: Discord is conflict; to discard is to throw away.

questions.passage: The band's early recordings sound joyful, but those years were full of ______. The two songwriters argued over every lyric, and the drummer quit and rejoined three times.
questions.explanation: Constant arguments and a drummer who kept quitting are conflict.

distractors.why: Consensus means agreement, the opposite of constant argument.
Alacrity means cheerful readiness, which does not describe quarrels.
Opulence means luxury, which is unrelated to the band's disagreements.
